summary: Initial discovery focused on model selection (open models vs managed), long context support, multilingual needs (EN/FR/ES), and VPC/private hosting constraints. Customer is leaning toward a Dedicated or Private deployment for data residency and auditability but wants hosted latency/cost comparisons. Agreed to pilot + security review.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript:
Header: 2026-03-27 11:00 PT | Duration: 42m | Recorded by: Fireflies
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CTO - Pioneer), Priya Patel (ML Eng), Sara Ng (Product)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the account, and Diego is our solutions engineer. Quick agenda, we'll run through your goals, current infra, talk model options — open models vs managed hosted — then deployment options (hosted, dedicated, private) and tool / function calling.

[00:24] Liam (Customer): Yeah thanks, uh quick context. We're building a customer support summarization and extraction pipeline plus a multilingual chat assistant. Data residency is important for some European customers, and we have strict audit requirements. We're evaluating if we should go hosted first or straight to dedicated/private.

[00:40] Priya (Customer): Also, we have some long documents — call transcripts and legal docs — so context length matters. We could need 32k to 64k windows for a subset of flows. And we want generation in EN/FR/ES, maybe PT later.

[00:58] Diego (Redwood SE): Got it. For the long context use case, there are a few levers: model choice (some open models support longer context natively), chunking + retrieval, and caching/kv cache for repeated prefixes. On Redwood's side, our runtime supports continuous KV cache and prefix caching which can reduce token costs while keeping latency SLOs.

[01:20] Sara (Customer): Sorry quick Q — when you say KV cache, do you mean the model's key-value cache or some Redwood layer?

[01:28] Diego: Good q — it's both. We manage the runtime KV-cache for decoding across requests and we also leverage model-specific attention caching; sometimes the terminology in docs gets messy, so you'll see K-V cash in older notes ;). That reduces recomputation if you have repeated context like system prompts.

[01:45] Liam: Budget is a constraint. Hosted is attractive for dev velocity, but we worry about per-token costs at scale. Dedicated seems predictable but needs a monthly commit. Private (VPC/on-prem) is compelling for the regulated customers.

[02:00] Maya: Totally — common tradeoff. We'll share a cost model comparing hosted per-token vs dedicated reserved capacity plus an expected sweet spot for when a customer should move to Dedicated. Diego, we'll show the numbers later.

[02:13] Diego: On model selection: for multilingual and long context, there are open models that are strong, like the big context variants of LlamaX-ish models and some specialized long-context models. We also recommend evaluating quantized checkpoints for CPU inference in private deployments. But note latency differences.

[02:38] Priya: We were also looking at Anthropic and OpenAI for baseline. Any notable differences for tool-calling/function calling? We need reliable structured outputs to call downstream microservices.

[02:50] Diego: Function/tool calling is supported across models via Redwood's structured output layer — we can route outputs into the toolchain. Some models are more deterministic; you may need evals and a small mapper. We have prebuilt integrations for webhook-style tool calls and a function-calling shim in the SDK. For private deployments we can run the same shim locally.

[03:12] Speaker 2 (maybe Liam): And what about streaming? We want progressive tokens to UI.

[03:18] Maya: Yes, streaming is supported across hosted/dedicated/private. Latency depends on model size and infra — e.g., a 70B quantized model on Dedicated can stream at decent latency for short prompts, but the long-context cases are heavier.

[03:36] Priya: Can you talk about model versioning and rollouts? We will iterate quickly and need to A/B test models and fallback strategies.

[03:45] Diego: Redwood Console supports model tagging and rollout policies, canary deploys, A/B splits, and automatic fallbacks if the chosen variant fails. You can pin model versions in your routes. For Private we ship a control plane that mirrors these features. Some of our customers run the control plane in their VPC for auditability.

[04:10] Sara: On compliance — specifically, do you integrate with our KMS and audit logs? We need encrypted keys and full traceability.

[04:18] Maya: Yes, for Private we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and provide audit logs. For Dedicated we offer encryption-at-rest and logs with SSO, RBAC, and long retention as an add-on. We'll include SOC2 and ISO docs in the follow-up.

[04:40] Liam: Good. How fast can we spin up a pilot? We want to run a small POC with 5–10k queries a day to validate latency and cost.

[04:50] Diego: Typical pilot is 2–4 weeks: we can provision a trial tenant on hosted or give a short-term Dedicated reservation. For Private on VPC it takes longer — network and security reviews usually add time. We can do a hybrid: host the control plane and run inference in your VPC as a first step.

[05:12] Priya: For multilingual accuracy, do you run eval suites? We have evaluation prompts and metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, human eval).

[05:22] Diego: We have built-in eval harnesses and can run model comparisons across your prompt set. We will run cross-model scoring and provide per-model latency/cost breakouts. Often open models win on cost but need prompt tuning.

[05:42] Maya: I'd like to surface a typical architecture we recommend: small encoder for retrieval+RAG, long-context specialized model for doc summarization, fallback to a higher-quality model for critical generation. Would that map to your flows?

[05:58] Liam: Yes, that seems reasonable. Our critical legal summarization needs higher-quality deterministic output; chat assistant can be a bit cheaper.

[06:10] Sara: Are there restrictions on model weights for Private? Some of the open weights have license terms.

[06:16] Diego: Correct, license screening is part of model onboarding. For private/on-prem we abide by model licenses and can suggest permissive open models. We'll flag models with restrictive licenses.

[06:30] Priya: On context windows: you mentioned 64k. Practically, which models in Redwood's catalog can handle that?

[06:36] Diego: We have a few curated entries that support 64k windows — call them LongContext-v* in the catalog — plus some 32k variants. Note: throughput drops as context size grows and memory config differs across GPU types. We'll include per-model perf profiles.

[06:58] Speaker 3 (Customer, muffled): Are there hard SLOs for latency? We need sub-second for short chat, and up to 3–5s for longer summarization is okay.

[07:10] Maya: Our Dedicated SLAs can be tuned. For hosted we publish median latency numbers; for Dedicated we can aim for strict P95 targets depending on commit and instance class. For private, latency depends on your infra but we advise the GPU shapes to hit your SLOs.

[07:30] Liam: One concern — network egress and cross-region data residency. Our EU customers must stay in EU. How do you handle region routing?

[07:38] Diego: We support region routing and smart routing policies. Requests for EU routes can be pinned to EU-hosted clusters or run in your VPC region. For Dedicated you can reserve capacity in a region.

[07:50] Priya: About tool-calling: we need typed outputs (JSON schemas) to call downstream services. How deterministic is that?

[07:58] Diego: Determinism depends on model and prompt engineering. We support function calling with enforced schemas and runtime validators; we also offer a post-processor step to coerce outputs to a schema and flag mismatches. That reduces false positives.

[08:22] Sara: For the pilot, we want to try two open models and one higher-cost managed model to compare quality. Is that feasible?

[08:29] Maya: Yes — that's our normal approach. We'll run an A/B across models using your prompts and provide a quality/latency/cost matrix. Diego will own the bench config.

[08:40] Diego: I'll propose a bench: Model A (open long-context 30B), Model B (open 70B quantized), Model C (hosted managed 30B equivalent). We'll measure end-to-end P95, token cost, and structured output compliance.

[09:00] Priya: We use Kafka and a microservices stack. Any prebuilt connectors?

[09:07] Diego: We have SDKs for Node/Python and a webhook connector that can push to Kafka via a lightweight adapter. For on-prem or VPC we can run the adapter inside your network.

[09:20] Liam: Security checklist — we need SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs, data retention controls, and the ability to purge customer data.

[09:30] Maya: All supported. For Private we put you in control of retention, and for Hosted/Dedicated we offer configurable retention policies and purge endpoints. We'll document the purge workflow in the follow-up.

[09:45] Sara: Any caveats around eval bias for multilingual? We worry English-optimized models underperform in FR/ES.

[09:55] Diego: Yes, you'll see variance. We'll run targeted multilingual evals. In some cases smaller regionally-tuned models outperform large global models; we'll surface recommendations.

[10:15] Maya: Quick pause — does anyone have pressing timeline constraints?

[10:20] Liam: We're aiming to start a pilot by mid-April to present results to leadership by May. So tight but doable.

[10:28] Diego: That timeline aligns with a 2–4 week pilot starting in early April. We'll need your prompt set and some sample traffic shapes.

[10:36] Priya: We'll share prompts and anonymized transcripts by Monday. Also want to know if Redwood can sign an initial DPA.

[10:43] Maya: Yes, we have a templated DPA; legal can fast-track. We'll send that along with the SOC2 artifact.

[10:54] Speaker (unknown): Slight background noise — sorry — but curious: if we need on-prem for some EU customers, do you support air-gapped installs?

[11:02] Diego: Yes, we have an on-prem package for air-gapped deployments; it requires a longer provisioning window and licensing review. Many enterprise customers do opt for that for regulated workloads.

[11:18] Priya: For monitoring, can we get token-level cost and trace to customer events?

[11:24] Diego: Redwood Console surfaces per-route per-model token breakdowns, token attribution by user id, and traces. We can export logs to your SIEM as well.

[11:36] Sara: Any gotchas— like licensing or model drift alerting?

[11:41] Diego: We have model registry alerts and quality regression monitors tied to eval sets. If a model regresses, we can trigger alerts and rollback. For licensing, we track model license types in the catalog.

[11:55] Maya: Let's recap next steps. We'll: 1) send SOC2 + security packet, DPA template; 2) Diego will prepare bench config and cost scenarios; 3) Pioneer to share prompt set & sample traffic; 4) schedule a DEEP SE session for private deployment network checklist.

[12:15] Liam: Sounds good. One last Q — what's your recommended starter config for Dedicated to hit sub-second chat latency?

[12:24] Diego: Depends on model, but commonly a couple of A100 or L4-like instances with 1–2 GPUs per node and small batching will hit sub-second for short prompts on a 13–30B model. We'll tailor the recommendation in the doc.

[12:40] Priya: Great. Thanks everyone.

[12:45] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and proposed timeline.

[12:50] End of recording.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hearings: 'K-V cash' for KV cache; 'Redwood Dedicate' for Dedicated; some overlaps and crosstalk.
